6.
The extension process

This section deals with a Ramsey theoretic construction pioneered by
Nešetřil and Rödl, who utilised it for
proving the
2
-uniform case of Theorem
1.4
for
g=4
in
[
24
]
.

The process is applied there in a rather concrete manner, exploiting that
every
C_{4}
-free bipartite graph
F
is expressible as an edge-disjoint union of stars,
any two of which intersect in at most one vertex. Such a decomposition of the set of
edges contains, of course, the same information as an equivalence relation on
E(F)

that regards any two edges of
F
to be equivalent if they pertain to the same star.
This perspective leads us to the concept of a pretrain and thereby to a rather general
abstract framework for discussing the extension process.

6.1.
Pretrains

A
pretrain
is a pair
(H,\equiv)
consisting of a
hypergraph
H
and an equivalence relation
\equiv
on
E(H)
.

If
H
is an ordered hypergraph, we call
(H,\equiv)

an
ordered pretrain
.

Similarly one defines the notion of an
f
-partite pretrain
.

A
wagon
of a pretrain
(H,\equiv)
is a subhypergraph of
H
without isolated
vertices whose set of edges forms an equivalence class of
\equiv
.

Definition 6.1
.

Given two pretrains
(F,\equiv^{F})
and
(H,\equiv^{H})
, the former is said to be
a
subpretrain
of the latter if

(

)

F
is a subhypergraph of
H

(

)

and any two edges of
F
are equivalent with respect to
\equiv^{F}
if
and only if they are equivalent with respect to
\equiv^{H}
.

Condition
( )
‣
6.1
is the only one that will occasionally receive further specifications.
For instance, it may happen that
F
is an induced subhypergraph of
H
and
then
(F,\equiv^{F})
is said to be an
induced subpretrain
of
(H,\equiv^{H})
.

If
(F,\equiv^{F})
and
(H,\equiv^{H})
are ordered pretrains, then for
(F,\equiv^{F})

to be an
ordered subpretrain
of
(H,\equiv^{H})
we require
( )
‣
6.1
to hold
in the stronger sense that
F
is an ordered subhypergraph of
H
.

A similar modification of
( )
‣
6.1
is required for
f
-partite subpretrains
.

The demand
( )
‣
6.1
tells us that
\equiv^{F}
is entirely determined by
F

and
\equiv^{H}
, and thus we shall frequently suppress the equivalence relation when
talking about subpretrains. Notice that when passing from
(H,\equiv^{H})

to
(F,\equiv^{F})
every wagon
W_{H}
of
H
either
vanishes
in the sense
that
E(W_{H})\cap E(F)=\varnothing
, or it
contracts
to a wagon
W_{F}
of
F

with
E(W_{F})=E(W_{H})\cap E(F)
.

It should be clear that every pretrain is a subpretrain of itself and that
the subpretrain relation is transitive.

A
system of pretrains
is a triple
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H})
consisting of a pretrain

(H,\equiv)
and of a collection
\mathscr{H}
of subpretrains of
(H,\equiv)
.

Moreover
\binom{(H,\equiv^{H})}{(F,\equiv^{F})}
refers to the collection of all
induced subpretrains of
(H,\equiv^{H})

isomorphic
to
(F,\equiv^{F})
, where
the notion of
pretrain isomorphism
is assumed to be self-explanatory.
The specifiers
\mathrm{n.n.i.}
,
\mathrm{pt}
, and
\mathrm{fpt}
may be
attached to
\binom{(H,\equiv^{H})}{(F,\equiv^{F})}

in the usual way. For
\mathscr{H}\subseteq\binom{(H,\equiv^{H})}{(F,\equiv^{F})}

and
r\in{\mathds{N}}
the partition relation

\mathscr{H}\longrightarrow(F,\equiv^{F})_{r}

means that no matter how the edges of
H
are coloured with
r
colours, there will
always exist a copy
(F_{\star},\equiv^{F_{\star}})\in\mathscr{H}
whose edges are the same colour.

To aid the readers orientation we remark that the induced Ramsey theorem does also hold
for pretrains in place of hypergraphs and that, in fact, this result can be shown by
means of the same partite construction (see Proposition
7.1
below).

6.2.
Extensions

For a concise description of the extension process we require a little bit of preparation.
First of all, suppose that we start with a pretrain
(F,\equiv^{F})
and enlarge its wagons
as disjointly as possible, thus obtaining a new pretrain
(H,\equiv^{H})
. We then say
that
(H,\equiv^{H})
is an extension of
(F,\equiv^{F})
. Let us say the same thing again
in a more precise way.

Definition 6.2
.

Given a subpretrain
(F,\equiv^{F})

(

vertices.

6.3.
Linear pretrains

There are two possible linearity conditions one can impose on pretrains
depending on whether one wants the edges or the wagons to avoid intersections
in two or more vertices. The linear pretrains considered in this article avoid
both possibilities at the same time.

Definition 6.9
.

A pretrain
(H,\equiv^{H})
is said to be

if

(

)

the hypergraph
H
is linear

(

)

and
|V(W^{\prime})\cap V(W^{\prime\prime})|\leq 1

any two distinct wagons
W^{\prime}
,
W^{\prime\prime}
.

A system of pretrains
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H})
is
linear
if its underlying
pretrain
(H,\equiv)
is linear.

For later use we record an easy consequence of linearity.

7.
Pretrains in partite constructions

We organise the material in this section in such a manner that it constitutes
a proof of the induced Ramsey theorem for pretrains. This result, however, only
serves as a point of reference and the arguments occurring in the proof will be more
relevant in the sequel than the theorem itself.

Proposition 7.1
.

Given an ordered
f
-partite pretrain
(F,\equiv^{F})
as well as a number of
colours
r
, there exists an ordered
f
-partite system of pretrains

(H,\equiv^{H},\mathscr{H})
such that

\mathscr{H}\longrightarrow(F,\equiv^{F})_{r}\,.

Observe that this result is incomparable in strength to Lemma
6.11
.
For instance, we defined constructions of the form
\mathrm{Ext}(\Omega,\Phi)
as applying
to linear pretrains only.
1
1

1

One can relax this requirement somewhat, but not
indefinitely.

On the other hand, the proof of Proposition
7.1
presented in
§
7.4
relies on a construction that often yields nonlinear
pretrains
(H,\equiv^{H})
even when the given pretrain
(F,\equiv^{F})
is linear.

7.1.
A partite lemma for pretrains

Let
(F,\equiv^{F})
be a
k
-partite
k
-uniform pretrain and let
r\in{\mathds{N}}

be a number of colours. The Hales-Jewett construction introduced in §
3.1

leads to a system
\mathrm{HJ}_{r}(F)=(H,\mathscr{H})
.

On
E(H)
we can define an equivalence relation
\equiv^{H}
by taking, essentially,
the product of the equivalence relations
\equiv^{F}
that we have on the “factors” of
H
.
More precisely, if
H
is the
n^{\mathrm{th}}
Hales-Jewett power of
F
and

\lambda\colon E(F)^{n}\longrightarrow E(H)
denotes the canonical
bijection, then we define

\lambda(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})\equiv^{H}\lambda(e^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,e^{\prime}_{n})\,\,\,\Longleftrightarrow\,\,\,\forall\nu\in[n]\,\,e_{\nu}\equiv^{F}e^{\prime}_{\nu}

for all
e_{1},\ldots,e_{n},e^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,e^{\prime}_{n}\in E(F)
.

Claim 7.2
.

If
F_{\star}\in\mathscr{H}
and
\equiv^{F_{\star}}
denotes the equivalence relation on

E(F_{\star})
rendering
(F,\equiv^{F})
and
(F_{\star},\equiv^{F_{\star}})
naturally
isomorphic, then
(F_{\star},\equiv^{F_{\star}})
is an induced subpretrain
of
(H,\equiv^{H})
.

Proof.

We already saw in Lemma
3.2
that
F_{\star}
is an induced subhypergraph
of
H
. It remains to show that any two edges of
F_{\star}
are equivalent with respect
to
\equiv^{F_{\star}}
if and only if they are equivalent with respect to
\equiv^{H}
.

Suppose that
F_{\star}
is given by the
combinatorial embedding
\eta\colon E(F)\longrightarrow E(F)^{n}
, which in
turn depends, as in the proof of Lemma
3.2
, on the partition
[n]=C\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}M

of
[n]
into constant and moving coordinates and on the
map
\widetilde{\eta}\colon C\longrightarrow E(F)
.

Let
e,e^{\prime}\in E(F)
be arbitrary and write
\eta(e)=(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})
as well
as
\eta(e^{\prime})=(e^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,e^{\prime}_{n})
. Now it remains to observe

\displaystyle(\lambda\circ\eta)(e)\equiv^{H}(\lambda\circ\eta)(e^{\prime})

\displaystyle\,\,\,\Longleftrightarrow\,\,\,\forall\nu\in[n]\,\,e_{\nu}\equiv e^{\prime}_{\nu}

\displaystyle\,\,\,\Longleftrightarrow\,\,\,\forall\nu\in M\,\,e_{\nu}\equiv e^{\prime}_{\nu}

\displaystyle\,\,\,\Longleftrightarrow\,\,\,e\equiv^{F}e^{\prime}\,,

where the last equivalence exploits
M\neq\varnothing
.
∎

Concerning notation, it seems best to denote the system of pretrains

\{(F_{\star},\equiv^{F_{\star}})\colon F_{\star}\in\mathscr{H}\}
by
\mathscr{H}
again,
so that we may refer to the system of pretrains
(H,\equiv^{H},\mathscr{H})
.
Besides, we write

\mathrm{HJ}_{r}(F,\equiv^{F})=(H,\equiv^{H},\mathscr{H})

for the above construction; so from now on
\mathrm{HJ}_{r}(\cdot)
applies
to pretrains as well.

7.2.

\mathscr{P}_{0}
become isomorphic to
(F,\equiv^{F})
as
pretrains,

\bullet

and edges belonging to different copies are nonequivalent
with respect to
\equiv_{0}
.

The second bullet may seem arbitrary at this moment, but proves to be useful later.
Essentially, there will be notions of cycles and
\mathfrak{Girth}
for systems of pretrains,
and in those cycles wagons can serve as connectors. Now if the wagons were allowed
to spread over several copies in
\mathscr{P}_{0}
, then we could jump from one copy to the
next using wagon connectors and already the
\mathfrak{Girth}
of picture zero could be out of
control.

7.3.
Partite amalgamations

Now suppose that
(\Pi,\equiv^{\Pi},\mathscr{P},\psi_{\Pi})

that

7.4.
Proof of Proposition
7.1

Given an ordered
f
-partite pretrain
(F,\equiv^{F})
together with a number of colours
r

we can construct the system
\mathrm{Rms}_{r}(F)=(G,\mathscr{G})
as in Section
3

and enumerate
E(G)=\{e(1),\ldots,e(N)\}
as usual. Starting with the pretrain picture
zero
(\Pi_{0},\equiv_{0},\mathscr{P}_{0},\psi_{0})
introduced in §
7.2
we
construct recursively a
sequence

(\Pi_{\alpha},\equiv_{\alpha},\mathscr{P}_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha})_{\alpha\leq N}

of pretrain pictures in the
expected way. That is, if the pretrain picture

(\Pi_{\alpha-1},\equiv_{\alpha-1},\mathscr{P}_{\alpha-1},\psi_{\alpha-1})

has just been constructed for some positive
\alpha\leq N
, we apply the pretrain
construction
\mathrm{HJ}_{r}(\cdot)
to its constituent over
e(\alpha)
, thus getting
a system of pretrains
(H_{\alpha},\equiv^{H_{\alpha}},\mathscr{H}_{\alpha})
, and as explained
in §
7.3
we construct the next pretrain picture

(\Pi_{\alpha},\equiv_{\alpha},\mathscr{P}_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha})=(\Pi_{\alpha-1},\equiv_{\alpha-1},\mathscr{P}_{\alpha-1},\psi_{\alpha-1})\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}}(H_{\alpha},\equiv^{H_{\alpha}},\mathscr{H}_{\alpha})\,.

For the usual reason, the final picture satisfies the partition relation

(\Pi_{N},\equiv_{N},\mathscr{P}_{N})\longrightarrow(F,\equiv^{F})_{r}\,,

and thereby Proposition
7.1
is proved. ∎

Similarly, whenever we have a Ramsey construction
\Phi
for hypergraphs and a
partite lemma
\Xi
for pretrains, we obtain the Ramsey construction
\mathrm{PC}(\Phi,\Xi)

applicable to pretrains. For instance, we can now regard
\mathrm{CPL}=\mathrm{PC}(\mathrm{HJ},\mathrm{HJ})
also
as a partite lemma for pretrains and then we can move on to the pretrain
construction
\Omega^{(2)}=\mathrm{PC}(\mathrm{Rms},\mathrm{CPL})
.

This construction provides an alternative
proof of Proposition
7.1
, which has the obvious advantage to yield systems
of pretrains whose underlying hypergraphs have clean intersections.

7.5.
Orientation

To motivate the material in the next two sections we would briefly like to discuss
the following problem, which seems rather important to us:
Given a linear pretrain
(F,\equiv^{F})
and a number of colours
r
,
can we find a linear system of pretrains
(H,\equiv^{H},\mathscr{H})

such that

\bullet

\mathscr{H}\longrightarrow(F,\equiv^{F})_{r}

\bullet

and any two copies in
\mathscr{H}
have a clean intersection?
(Recall that due to the linearity of
F
this means, roughly speaking,
that any two copies intersect “at most in an edge”—cf. the discussion
before Lemma
3.13
).

As the aforementioned construction
\Omega^{(2)}
yields such clean intersections,
it may be tempting to just set
(H,\equiv^{H},\mathscr{H})=\Omega^{(2)}_{r}(F,\equiv^{F})
.
However, it can happen for linear pretrains
(F,\equiv^{F})
that the
pretrain
(H,\equiv^{H})
obtained by means of
\Omega^{(2)}
fails to be linear.
Indeed, Corollary
3.14
only tells us that the hypergraph
H
needs to
be linear, but there is no reason why any two wagons of
\equiv^{H}
should intersect
in at most one vertex. As a matter of fact, it could be shown that already our initial
construction
\mathrm{HJ}
does not preserve this kind of linearity
and the same holds for the constructions
\mathrm{CPL}
and
\Omega^{(2)}
derived from it.

Fortunately we already know a pretrain construction
yielding linear pretrains, namely
\mathrm{Ext}(\Omega^{(2)},\Omega^{(2)})

(see Lemma
6.11
and the eight-step definition preceding it).
But the copies provided by this construction can intersect in entire wagons and,
hence, their intersections are in general quite far from being clean.
The method of the present subsection suggests a way to remedy this situation by
looking instead at the
construction
\mathrm{PC}\bigl(\Omega^{(2)},\mathrm{Ext}(\Omega^{(2)},\Omega^{(2)})\bigr)
.
At this moment, however, it is not yet clear whether this is a sensible construction,
for it is difficult to foresee whether at some moment we encounter a picture whose
constituents are nonlinear pretrains,
in which case it would be impossible to apply the partite lemma

\mathrm{Ext}(\Omega^{(2)},\Omega^{(2)})
.

An important insight we shall only gain in Section
9
is that actually this
obstruction does not arise.
So, in other words,
\mathrm{PC}\bigl(\Omega^{(2)},\mathrm{Ext}(\Omega^{(2)},\Omega^{(2)})\bigr)

applied to a linear pretrain yields a linear Ramsey pretrain and it is immediately
clear that this construction solves our problem.

8.
Basic properties of
\mathfrak{Girth}

In systems of pretrains there are certain undesirable kinds of
“short cyclic configurations of copies”, such as two copies intersecting
the same two wagons in edges, but these cannot be detected by Girth
as defined in §
4.2
. The goal of the present section is to define
and study a concept of
\mathfrak{Girth}
applicable to systems of pretrains which, roughly
speaking, takes care of cyclic configurations of copies that become visible at
the level of wagons. In the next section, we shall then see that
\mathfrak{Girth}
is highly
compatible both with the extension process and with the partite construction method.

8.1.
Basic concepts

Recall that a linear system of hypergraphs has small
\mathrm{Girth}

if all its cycles of copies of low order have one of two properties rendering
them negligible: either they fail to be semitidy or they have a master copy.
In the same way we shall define a system of pretrains to have small
\mathfrak{Girth}

if all its so-called big cycles of low order behave similarly.
The notion of a big cycle is defined as follows.

Definition 8.1
.

A
big cycle
in a system of pretrains
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H})
is a cyclic sequence

\mathscr{C}=F_{1}q_{1}F_{2}q_{2}\ldots F_{n}q_{n}

with
n\geq 2
satisfying the following conditions.

(
B1
)

The
copies

F_{1},\ldots,F_{n}
are in
\mathscr{H}
and we
have
F_{i}\neq F_{i+1}
for every
i\in{\mathds{Z}}/n{\mathds{Z}}
.

(
B2
)

The
connectors

q_{1},\ldots,q_{n}
are distinct and each of them
is either a vertex or a wagon of
(H,\equiv)
.

(
B3
)

If
i\in{\mathds{Z}}/n{\mathds{Z}}
and
q_{i}
is a vertex,
then
q_{i}\in V(F_{i})\cap V(F_{i+1})
.

(
B4
)

If
i\in{\mathds{Z}}/n{\mathds{Z}}
and
q_{i}
is a wagon,
then
E(q_{i})\cap E(F_{i})\neq\varnothing
and
E(q_{i})\cap E(F_{i+1})\neq\varnothing
.

The main difference between big cycles and the cycles of copies introduced
in Definition
4.3
is that now wagons rather than edges act as
connectors, which causes a corresponding change in the fourth condition
from
(

⁢
L
4

)
to
(

⁢
B
4

)
. A similar modification allows us to define the order
of a big cycle.
Notably, if
\mathscr{C}=F_{1}q_{1}\ldots F_{n}q_{n}
is a big cycle, we call an
index
i\in{\mathds{Z}}/n{\mathds{Z}}

\bullet

pure
if either both of
q_{i-1}
and
q_{i}
are wagons or both are
vertices and

\bullet

mixed
if one of
q_{i-1}
and
q_{i}
is a wagon while the other
one is a vertex,

and then we call the integer

\mathrm{ord}(\mathscr{C})=\big|\{i\in{\mathds{Z}}/n{\mathds{Z}}\colon i\text{ is pure}\}\big|+\tfrac{1}{2}\big|\{i\in{\mathds{Z}}/n{\mathds{Z}}\colon i\text{ is mixed}\}\big|

the
order
of
\mathscr{C}
.

Extended systems can be introduced in the same way as in Section
4
.
Explicitly, if
(H,\equiv)
is a pretrain, then every edge
e\in E(H)
gives rise
to a subpretrain with vertex set
e
, having
e
as its only edge, and endowed with the
only possible equivalence relation. There cannot arise confusion if we denote this
subpretrain again by
e^{+}
. Moreover, we keep using the notation
E^{+}(H)
for

\{e^{+}\colon e\in E(H)\}
, but this time meaning the collection of all subpretrains
of
(H,\equiv)
of the form
e^{+}
. Besides, if
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H})
is a system of
pretrains, we shall again write
\mathscr{H}^{+}=\mathscr{H}\cup E^{+}(H)
and call
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})

an
extended system of pretrains
.

Finally, we keep referring to copies of the
form
e^{+}
as
edge copies
,

while other copies of extended systems of pretrains will be
called
real copies
.

The
M(f)
-notation we have already seen in
Section
4
can now be applied to wagons.

Definition 8.2
.

Given a big cycle
\mathscr{C}=F_{1}q_{1}\ldots F_{n}q_{n}

in an extended system of pretrains
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})
we set

M^{\mathscr{C}}(W)=\bigl\{i\in{\mathds{Z}}/n{\mathds{Z}}\colon\text{$q_{i}$ is a vertex and $q_{i}\in V(W)$}\bigr\}

for every wagon

(H,\equiv)
. If
\mathscr{C}
is clear from the context,
we may omit it and just write

instead.

The semitidy cycles of copies considered earlier lead us to acceptable
big cycles.

A big cycle

\mathscr{C}=F_{1}q_{1}\ldots F_{n}q_{n}

in an extended system of pretrains

(

, then at least one copy of

is real.

(

, then there exists some

.

q_{i}

F_{i+2}

Let us offer two reasons why we believe that acceptability is a natural concept.
First, it turns out in Claim

below that if all wagons consist

Moreover, if
{M(W)=\{1,n-1\}}

The natural generalisation of master copies to the present context allows to collapse

We are now sufficiently prepared for the central concept of this section.
Recall that in Definition
6.9
we defined a system of pretrains to be
linear if its underlying pretrain is linear, which in turn means that neither
edges nor wagons can intersect in more than one vertex.

Definition 8.9
.

Given an extended system of pretrains
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})
as well as a
positive integer
g
we write
\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})>g
if

\bullet

the pretrain
(H,\equiv)
is linear

\bullet

and every acceptable big cycle
\mathscr{C}
in
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})

whose order is at most
g
has a supreme copy.

Let us clarify that the notions “acceptability” and “supreme copy” are defined
in all systems of pretrains no matter whether they are linear or not. Accordingly,
one can also ask for nonlinear systems whether they satisfy the statement “every big cycle
of order at most
g
has a supreme copy”. The answer can very well be affirmative for
a system
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})
that fails to be linear, but in such cases we do
not regard
\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})>g
as being true.

Example 8.10
.

Let
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})
be an extended linear system of pretrains.
Up to symmetry big cycles of order

\mathscr{C}=F_{1}xF_{2}W
,

)

(

⁢

)

are edge copies.
This configuration is tantamount to a vertex

in

As a matter of fact, we only impose condition

⁢

1

)

of

Next, we figure out what it means to say
that

For later reference we summarise this discussion as follows.

Lemma 8.11
.

Given an extended linear system of pretrains
(H,\equiv^{H},\mathscr{H}^{+})
the following
two statements are equivalent.

(

)

\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv^{H},\mathscr{H}^{+})>1
;

(

)

For every big cycle

f_{1}\in E(F_{1})\cap E(W)\quad\text{ and }\quad f_{2}\in E(F_{2})\cap E(W)

Suppose first that

‣

If

and if

For the converse direction we let

(

⁢

)

. ∎

\mathfrak{Girth}
relates to strong inducedness in the following way.

Lemma 8.14
.

If an extended system of pretrains
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})
satisfies

then every edge

Notice that due to the linearity of

from the assumption

.

Proof of Lemma
8.14
.

Suppose that
x,y\in V(F_{\star})\cap f

are distinct.
If
F_{\star}=f^{+}
, then
f\in E(F_{\star})
is clear, so suppose
F_{\star}\neq f^{+}
from
now on. The big cycle
\mathscr{C}=F_{\star}xf^{+}y
is acceptable, its order is
2
and,
therefore, it possesses a supreme copy. By Remark
8.8
(0 )

this supreme copy can only be

and the existence of an edge containing

and

ensures that

collapses to a short piece

with

.
Since

and thus we have indeed

.
∎

We conclude our list of preliminary observations on
\mathfrak{Girth}
as follows.

Fact 8.15
.

If a big cycle
\mathscr{C}
in an extended linear system of pretrains has a supreme
copy
F_{\star}
, then all vertex connectors of
\mathscr{C}
belong to
F_{\star}
.

Proof.

Let
q_{i}
be a vertex connector of
\mathscr{C}=F_{1}q_{1}\dots F_{n}q_{n}
. Due to
(

⁢
B
1

)

at least one of the copies
F_{i}
,
F_{i+1}
is distinct from
F_{\star}
, so by symmetry
we may assume
F_{i}\neq F_{\star}
. Consider the
F_{\star}
-piece
P_{i}
to which
F_{i}

collapses. If
P_{i}=f^{+}
is short, then
q_{i}\in f\subseteq V(F_{\star})
follows.
Similarly, if
P_{i}=(f^{\prime})^{+}W(f^{\prime\prime})^{+}
is long, then we have
q_{i}\in f^{\prime\prime}\subseteq V(F_{\star})
.
∎

8.2.
Special cases

The next item on our agenda are simplified characterisations of

\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})
applicable to systems of pretrains with special properties.
First, the simplest case for
\mathscr{H}^{+}
is that
\mathscr{H}^{+}=E^{+}(H)
and we address this
situation in Lemma
8.17
below. Second, the case where
\mathscr{H}^{+}
is arbitrary
and every wagon consists of a single edge is dealt with in Lemma
8.18
;
it turns out that
\mathfrak{Girth}
is then essentially the same as
\mathrm{Girth}
.

Definition 8.16
.

For a pretrain
(H,\equiv)
and an integer
g\geq 2
we write

\mathfrak{girth}(H,\equiv)>g
if
H
is linear and
the girth of the set system one obtains from
(H,\equiv)

upon replacing the wagons by new edges (and deleting the original edges)
exceeds
g
.

Due to Fact
4.1
this means, explicitly, that if for some
n\in[2,g]
we have
a cyclic sequence
W_{1}q_{1}\ldots W_{n}q_{n}
such that

\bullet

W_{1},\ldots,W_{n}
are wagons of
(H,\equiv)
,

\bullet

the vertices
q_{1},\ldots,q_{n}
of
H
are distinct,

\bullet

and
q_{i}\in V(W_{i})\cap V(W_{i+1})
holds for every
i\in{\mathds{Z}}/n{\mathds{Z}}
,

then
W_{1}=\dots=W_{n}
.
Notice that a pretrain
(H,\equiv)
is linear in the sense
of Definition
6.9
if and only if
\mathfrak{girth}(H,\equiv)>2
.

Let us emphasise that the lowercase “
\mathfrak{g}
” in Definition
8.16
as
opposed to the capital “
\mathfrak{G}
” in Definition
8.9
indicates that
here we deal with individual objects as opposed to the systems treated there. So the rule
on capitalisation is the same as in Section
4
. It might further be helpful
to bear in mind that German letters highlight the importance of equivalence relations
on the edge sets, while Roman letters are used in cases where such pretrain structures
are absent or ignored.

Lemma 8.17
.

If
(H,\equiv)
is a linear pretrain and
g\geq 2
, then

\mathfrak{girth}(H,\equiv)>g\,\Longleftrightarrow\,\mathfrak{Girth}\bigl(H,\equiv,E^{+}(H)\bigr)>g\,\Longleftrightarrow\,\mathfrak{Girth}\bigl(H,\equiv,E^{+}(H)\cup\{(H,\equiv)\}\bigr)>g\,.

Proof.

Evidently, the last condition implies the middle one. Conversely, the middle
condition also implies the last one, for
(H,\equiv)
is a supreme copy of every big
cycle in the system of pretrains
\bigl(H,\equiv,E^{+}(H)\cup\{(H,\equiv)\}\bigr)

that contains
(H,\equiv)
. It therefore remains to show that the first and
middle statement are equivalent.

Suppose first that
\mathfrak{Girth}\bigl(H,\equiv,E^{+}(H)\bigr)>g
, but that for some
n\in[2,g]

there exists a cyclic sequence
W_{1}q_{1}\ldots W_{n}q_{n}
violating
\mathfrak{girth}(H,\equiv)>g
.
If we choose this counterexample with
n
as small as possible,
then
W_{1},\ldots,W_{n}
are distinct. Moreover, the linearity of
(H,\equiv)

yields
n\geq 3
.

Let us select for every index
i\in{\mathds{Z}}/n{\mathds{Z}}
a piece
P_{i}
as follows. If there
exists an edge
f_{i}\in W_{i}
with
q_{i-1},q_{i}\in f_{i}
, then let
P_{i}=f_{i}^{+}
.
If there is no such edge, then we pick edges
f^{\prime}_{i},f^{\prime\prime}_{i}\in E(W_{i})
with

q_{i-1}\in f^{\prime}_{i}
and
q_{i}\in f^{\prime\prime}_{i}
, which is possible due to the fact that wagons
have no isolated vertices. Moreover, the absence of
f_{i}
entails
f^{\prime}_{i}\neq f^{\prime\prime}_{i}

and thus
P_{i}=(f^{\prime}_{i})^{+}W_{i}(f^{\prime\prime}_{i})^{+}
is a long piece. Now
\mathscr{C}=P_{1}q_{1}\ldots P_{n}q_{n}

is a big cycle in
\bigl(H,\equiv,E^{+}(H)\bigr)
with
\mathrm{ord}(\mathscr{C})=n\in[3,g]
.
By
n\geq 3
it has the property
(

⁢
A
1

)
of acceptability
and one checks easily that
any violation of
(

⁢
A
2

)
or
(

⁢
A
3

)
would yield a contradiction to the minimality
of
n
. Thus
\mathscr{C}
is acceptable and Definition
8.5
entails that
\mathscr{C}

has a supreme copy. However,
\mathscr{C}
does not even contain a real copy, so we
arrive at a contradiction to Remark
8.8
(0 )
.

It remains to prove that, conversely, assuming
\mathfrak{girth}(H,\equiv)>g

we can derive

\mathfrak{Girth}\bigl(H,\equiv,E^{+}(H)\bigr)>g\,.

Consider any acceptable big cycle

\mathscr{C}=f_{1}^{+}q_{1}\ldots f_{n}^{+}q_{n}
in
\bigl(H,\equiv,E^{+}(H)\bigr)
with
\mathrm{ord}(\mathscr{C})\leq g
.
Due to
(

⁢
A
1

)
the order of
\mathscr{C}
is at least
2
.
Notice that owing to
(

⁢
B
2

)
and
(

⁢
B
4

)
is cannot be the case that two
consecutive connectors of
\mathscr{C}
are wagons. Therefore, the order of
\mathscr{C}

is the number of its vertex connectors. By symmetry we may suppose that

1\leq i(1)<i(2)<\ldots<i(m)=n

are the indices of the vertex connectors of
\mathscr{C}
,
where
m=\mathrm{ord}(\mathscr{C})\in[2,g]
. As
q_{1}
and
q_{2}
cannot be consecutive wagons,

is either
1
or
2
and in both cases there exists a wagon
W_{1}
containing all edges

f_{i}
with
i\in[1,i(1)]
. Similarly, for every

The next result essentially says that if every edge is its own wagon, then
\mathfrak{Girth}
is the same
as
\mathrm{Girth}
.

Lemma 8.18
.

Let
(H,\mathscr{H})
be a linear system and let
g\geq 2
be a natural number.
If
\equiv
denotes the equivalence relation on

whose equivalence classes are
single edges, then

\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{H}^{+})>g\,\,\,\Longleftrightarrow\,\,\,\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})>g\,.

Proof.

For simplicity we treat cycles of copies in
(H,\mathscr{H}^{+})
as if they were big cycles
in
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})
and vice versa.
Pedantically speaking, this is not quite precise, for in the former case the
non-vertex connectors are just edges of

, while in the latter
case they are wagons and thus of the form

with

. Moreover,
in the former case the copies are just subhypergraphs of

belonging to
\mathscr{H}^{+}
,
whereas in the latter case they are, officially, subpretrains of
(H,\equiv)

and thus accompanied by equivalence relations on their sets of
edges.
Ignoring these extremely minor differences it will be convenient
to identify the two concepts for the current purposes; thus when speaking
of cycles in the remainder of this proof we shall mean either cycles of copies
in
(H,\mathscr{H}^{+})
or the corresponding big cycles in
(H,\equiv,\mathscr{H}^{+})
.
It turns out that there is a quite literal translation from
Definition
4.17
to Definition
8.9
.

A cycle has a master copy if and only if it has a supreme copy.

9.
\mathfrak{Girth}
in constructions

As we shall see in this section, the extension process and partite constructions
are in perfect harmony with
\mathfrak{Girth}
.

9.1.
The extension lemma

Roughly speaking, we shall prove now that the extension process described in
Section
6
converts
\mathrm{Girth}
into
\mathfrak{Girth}
—in the sense that if a
hypergraph construction
\Psi
yields systems with large
\mathrm{Girth}
, then the
pretrain construction
\mathrm{Ext}(\Phi,\Psi)
yields systems with
large
\mathfrak{Girth}
, provided that
\Phi
generates strongly induced copies.
In other words, German
\mathfrak{Girth}
seems to be the correct notion for analysing
cycles in systems of pretrains obtained by means of the extension process.

Lemma 9.1
.

Suppose that
g\geq 2
,

\bullet

\Phi

\bullet

The proof of any statement addressing pretrain systems of

9.2.

The next result and its proof share strong similarities with the material in

Proposition 9.14
.

Suppose that
g\geq 2
and that
\Xi

\bullet

applicable to
k

The following should now be straightforward, but let us elaborate.

Proof of Proposition
9.14
.

Consider a pretrain
(F,\equiv^{F})
with
\mathfrak{girth}(F,\equiv^{F})>g
and a
number of colours

\Phi_{r}(F)=(G,\mathscr{G})

corresponding to this situation satisfies

{\mathfrak{Girth}(\Pi_{0},\equiv_{0},\mathscr{P}_{0}^{+})>g}

Starting with picture zero we intend to execute a partite construction, i.e., to
construct recursively a sequence of pictures

(\Pi_{\alpha},\equiv_{\alpha},\mathscr{P}_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha})_{\alpha\leq N}

over
(G,\mathscr{G})
.
Suppose that for some
\alpha\in[N]
we have just constructed a picture

(\Pi_{\alpha-1},\equiv_{\alpha-1},\mathscr{P}_{\alpha-1},\psi_{\alpha-1})
with

\mathfrak{Girth}(\Pi_{\alpha-1},\equiv_{\alpha-1},\mathscr{P}_{\alpha-1}^{+})>g\,.

In particular, we have

\mathfrak{Girth}\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha-1},\equiv_{\alpha-1},E^{+}(\Pi_{\alpha-1})\bigr)>g

and Lemma
8.17
reveals

\mathfrak{girth}(\Pi_{\alpha-1},\equiv_{\alpha-1})>g\,.

This in turn implies that
\Xi_{r}(\cdot)
applies to the
constituent

\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha-1}^{e(\alpha)},\equiv_{\alpha-1}^{e(\alpha)}\bigr)
,
where
\equiv_{\alpha-1}^{e(\alpha)}
denotes the restriction
of
\equiv_{\alpha-1}

to
E\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha-1}^{e(\alpha)}\bigr)
. In other words,

\Xi_{r}\bigl(\Pi_{\alpha-1}^{e(\alpha)},\equiv_{\alpha-1}^{e(\alpha)}\bigr)=(H_{\alpha},\equiv^{H_{\alpha}},\mathscr{H}_{\alpha})

is defined and satisfies
\mathfrak{Girth}(H_{\alpha},\equiv^{H_{\alpha}},\mathscr{H}_{\alpha}^{+})>g
.
By Lemma
9.15
the new picture

(\Pi_{\alpha},\equiv_{\alpha},\mathscr{P}_{\alpha},\psi_{\alpha})=(\Pi_{\alpha-1},\equiv_{\alpha-1},\mathscr{P}_{\alpha-1}\psi_{\alpha-1})\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}}(H_{\alpha},\equiv^{H_{\alpha}},\mathscr{H}_{\alpha})

has the property
\mathfrak{Girth}(\Pi_{\alpha},\equiv_{\alpha},\mathscr{P}_{\alpha}^{+})>g

and thus the partite construction goes on.

Eventually we obtain the final picture

\mathrm{PC}(\Phi,\Xi)_{r}(F,\equiv^{F})=(\Pi_{N},\equiv_{N},\mathscr{P}_{N})
with

\mathfrak{Girth}(\Pi_{N},\equiv_{N},\mathscr{P}_{N}^{+})>g\,.\qed

9.3.
Orientation

The main results of this section lead to a quick solution of the problem
discussed in §
7.5
. The construction

\varUpsilon=\mathrm{Ext}(\Omega^{(2)},\Omega^{(2)})
applies to all linear, ordered,

f
-partite

pretrains. Due to the case
g=2
of Lemma
9.1
the systems of pretrains

(H,\equiv^{H},\mathscr{H})
generated by
\varUpsilon
satisfy
\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv^{H},\mathscr{H}^{+})>2

(the hypotheses of this lemma were verified in Proposition
3.8

and Corollary
5.6
).

Now we can use
\varUpsilon
as a partite lemma and look at the
construction
\Lambda=\mathrm{PC}(\Omega^{(2)},\varUpsilon)
. The case
g=2

of Proposition
9.14
informs us that for every linear,
ordered,
f
-partite pretrain
(F,\equiv^{F})
and every number of
colours
r
the system of pretrains
\Lambda_{r}(F,\equiv^{F})=(H,\equiv^{H},\mathscr{H})

is defined and satisfies
\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv^{H},\mathscr{H}^{+})>2
. So, in particular,

(H,\equiv^{H})
is a linear pretrain arrowing
(F,\equiv^{F})
with
r
colours.
Moreover, and this is the main advantage of
\Lambda
over
\varUpsilon
, the copies
in
\mathscr{H}
have clean intersections due to Lemma
3.4
.

10.
Trains

Let us start this section with an observation of central importance to our
girth Ramsey theoretic endeavour: a “typical”
k
-partite
k
-uniform hypergraph
can never occur as a constituent of a picture that arises when the partite
construction method is carried out over a linear system
(G,\mathscr{G})
.

For instance, all constituents of picture zero consist of a matching together with
some isolated vertices (cf. Figure
3.2
). The first picture is obtained by
applying the intended partite lemma to the constituent over some edge
e(1)\in E(G)

and performing the usual amalgamation.
Evidently, every constituent of the new picture over an edge
e\in E(G)

with
e(1)\cap e=\varnothing
is still a matching augmented by some isolated vertices.
More interestingly, if an edge
e\neq e(1)

intersects
e(1)
, then by the linearity of
G
this intersection occurs in a single
vertex
x
and, accordingly,
the new constituent over
e
is obtained by taking several disjoint copies of the old
constituent and identifying a couple of vertices on the music line
V_{x}
. However, there
occur no such identifications on the other music lines
V_{z}
with
z\in e\smallsetminus\{x\}
.
Notice that we can endow the new constituent with a pretrain structure
by declaring two edges to be equivalent if they belong to the same copy of the old
constituent.
It should also be clear that this pretrain is going to be linear if our partite
lemma delivers copies with clean intersections.

Similarly, the most complicated possibility for a constituent of the second picture
is that one takes plenty of disjoint copies of such a pretrain and identifies some
of their vertices, all identified vertices belonging to a common music line.
As the partite construction progresses, there iteratively arise more and more complex
objects all of which fit into the framework we shall now develop (see also
Figure
2.3
).

10.1.
Quasitrains and parameters

We begin by encoding the recursive formation of our
objects in terms of a sequence of nested equivalence relations.

Definition 10.1
.

Given a positive integer
m
we say that

\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}=(F,\equiv_{0},\ldots,\equiv_{m})

Every wagon of the pretrain

(

(

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle F\hfil

.

Example 10.2
.

Quasitrains of height
1
are triples
(F,\equiv_{0},\equiv_{1})
, where

is a hypergraph, the
0

are single edges
(by
( )
‣

and all edges belong to the same

( )
‣

). Consequently, there is a natural bijective correspondence
between quasitrains of height

and hypergraphs. At a later moment it will be
convenient to call

the quasitrain of height
1

associated with
the hypergraph

.

Example 10.3
.

Similarly, quasitrains of height
2
are quadruples

(F,\equiv_{0},\equiv_{1},\equiv_{2})

with the properties that
(F,\equiv_{0},\equiv_{2})
is a quasitrain of height

and
(F,\equiv_{1})
is a pretrain. In particular, quasitrains of height

are in natural bijective correspondence with pretrains.

The train concept to which we proceed next is taking into account what

When compared to the discussion at the beginning of this section,
there are two directions in which our definition of trains might
appear to be too general.
First, we only motivated the need for
k
-partite
k
-uniform
trains, whereas Definition
10.4
allows the underlying hypergraphs of trains
to be
f
-partite for general functions
f
. The reason for this is that we intend
to subject trains to the extension process and, as we saw in Section
6
,
when we apply a construction of the form
\mathrm{Ext}(\Phi,\Psi)
to a
k
-partite

k
-uniform pretrain, the construction
\Psi
needs to be applicable to
general
f
-partite hypergraphs.

Another surprise in Definition
10.4
might be that we allow the sets

A_{1},\dots,A_{m}
constituting the parameter of the train to be arbitrary subsets
of
I
.
After all, we have just tried to convey the idea that for trains created by partite
constructions we can demand
|A_{\mu}|\leq 1
for every
\mu\in[m]
, and that this
very fact will be responsible for the girth increment the achievement of which
is the reason for starting to consider trains at all.
On the other hand, when we have some construction applicable to
f
-partite trains
and attempt to clean it by means of the partite construction method, then from the
point of view of the constituents of the involved pictures the sizes of the
sets in the parameter can appear to have been enlarged.
This tension between conflicting demands on
the parameters will completely resolve itself in Section
12
.

It is probably clear what we mean by subtrains, but let us elaborate for the sake of
completeness.

Definition 10.6

The subtrain relation is, of course, reflexive and transitive.
A

.

It will be convenient to denote this system by
(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}},\mathscr{H})
as well.
We regard the notion of an
extended quasitrain system

(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}},\mathscr{H}^{+})

to be self-explanatory.

10.2.
More German girth

Next we need to generalise
\mathfrak{girth}
to quasitrains, and
\mathfrak{Girth}
to
systems of quasitrains. In both contexts we work with the free monoid
\mathfrak{M}

generated by
{\mathds{N}}_{\geq 2}
.
Thus the elements of
\mathfrak{M}
can be thought of as sequences of elements
from
{\mathds{N}}_{\geq 2}
and the composition of
\mathfrak{M}
, denoted by
\circ
,
is the concatenation of sequences.
The
empty sequence

\varnothing
is the neutral element of
\mathfrak{M}
.
For a sequence
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}=(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})\in\mathfrak{M}
we call
m=|\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}|

the
length
of

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle g\hfil

and we use
\inf(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}})
as an abbreviation
for
\inf\{g_{1},\dots,g_{m}\}
.
So we have
\inf(\varnothing)=\infty
and in all other cases the infimum is just
a minimum.
For integers
g\geq 2
and
m\geq 1
the sequence
(g,\dots,g)
consisting
of
m
terms equal to
g
is the
m^{\mathrm{th}}
power of the one-term sequence
(g)

and thus we shall denote it by
(g)^{m}
.
Finally, we write
\mathfrak{M}_{\leq}
for the subset of
\mathfrak{M}
consisting of all nondecreasing
sequences (including
\varnothing
), and we set
\mathfrak{M}^{\times}_{\leq}=\mathfrak{M}_{\leq}\smallsetminus\{\varnothing\}
.

Lemma 10.8
.

be given.
If
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}=(F,\equiv_{0}^{F},\ldots,\equiv_{m}^{F})

\mathrm{girth}(F)>g_{1}
.

Proof.

The case
\mu=m
is clear, for by Definition
10.1
( )
‣
10.1

there is only one
m
-wagon of

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle F\hfil

and by Definition
10.7

applied to that wagon we obtain indeed
\mathfrak{girth}(F,\equiv_{m-1})>g_{m}
.

Arguing by decreasing induction
on
\mu
we now assume that some
\mu\in[m-1]
has the property

\mathfrak{girth}(F,\equiv_{\mu})>g_{\mu+1}\geq g_{\mu}
, meaning that the
\mu
-wagons
of

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle F\hfil

form a set system whose girth exceeds
g_{\mu}
.
According to Definition
10.7
each of these
\mu
-wagons is composed of

(\mu-1)
-wagons the vertex sets of which form a set system whose girth
is larger than
g_{\mu}
as well. Due to Fact
4.2
this
implies
\mathfrak{girth}(F,\equiv_{\mu-1})>g_{\mu}

and the induction is complete.

As the
0
-wagons consist of single edges, the special case
\mu=1

yields
\mathrm{girth}(F)>g_{1}
.
∎

The reason why we are keeping track of suitable parameters when discussing trains
is that they are needed for the following important yet innocent looking variant of
this argument.

Lemma 10.9
.

Let
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}=(F,\equiv_{0},\ldots,\equiv_{m})
be a
k
-partite

k
-uniform train whose parameter
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle B\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle B\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle B\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle B\hfil$\crcr}}}=(B_{1},\dots,B_{m})

satisfies
|B_{\mu}|\leq 1
for every
\mu\in[m]
.
If
\mathfrak{girth}(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}})>(g)^{m}
holds for some integer
g\geq 2
,
then
\mathrm{girth}(F)>g+1
.

Proof.

We are to prove that the girth of the unique
m
-wagon of
F
exceeds
g+1
.
Arguing indirectly, we let
\mu\in[0,m]
be minimal with the property that
for some
\mu
-wagon
W_{\mu}
of

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle F\hfil

the statement
\mathrm{girth}(W_{\mu})>g+1
fails.

As the
0
-wagons of

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle F\hfil

are single edges, we have
\mu>0
. Therefore
W_{\mu}

is comprised of
(\mu-1)
-wagons and by the minimality of
\mu
the girth of each of
them is larger than
g+1
. According to Definition
10.7
the vertex sets
of these
(\mu-1)
-wagons form a set system whose girth is larger than
g
.
Due to Fact
4.2
it follows that
W_{\mu}
contains a
(g+1)
-cycle

e_{1}v_{1}\ldots e_{g+1}v_{g+1}
and
distinct
(\mu-1)
-wagons
W^{1}_{\mu-1},\ldots,W^{g+1}_{\mu-1}

with
e_{i}\subseteq V(W^{i}_{\mu-1})
for every
i\in{\mathds{Z}}/(g+1){\mathds{Z}}
.
Now clause
( )
‣
10.4
of Definition
10.4

implies
v_{1},\ldots,v_{g+1}\in V_{B_{\mu}}
. Together with
|B_{\mu}|\leq 1

this shows, in particular, that
v_{1}
,
v_{g+1}
are in the same vertex
class of
F
. On the other hand, these two vertices are distinct and belong
to the edge
e_{1}
. We have thereby reached a contradiction to the assumption
that
F
be
k
-partite and
k
-uniform for some
k\geq 2
, and the proof is complete.
∎

10.10
this shows

{\mathfrak{Girth}(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}},\mathscr{H}^{+})>(2)}
and altogether the system

(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}},\mathscr{H})
is as demanded by
\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(2)}
.
This concludes our discussion of the case that
F
has no isolated vertices.

In the general case we remove the isolated vertices from
F
,
perform the construction we have just seen, and then we put the isolated
vertices back.
This needs to be done in such a way that each copy in
\mathscr{H}
ends up getting
its own isolated vertices, so that
\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv^{H}_{1},\mathscr{H}^{+})>1
remains valid.
∎

There will be two quite distinct kinds of induction steps for
traversing
\mathfrak{M}_{\leq}^{\times}
.
First, the extension process together with some subsequent cleaning steps
will allow us to prove the following implication.

Proposition 10.14
.

For every nonempty nondecreasing sequence
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\leq}^{\times}
the
principle
\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}}
implies

.

Second, we shall later describe a diagonal variant of the
partite construction method and establish the following result.

.

\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\leq}

\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}}

and
\inf(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}})\geq g+1
is given.
Iterative applications of the induction hypothesis
establish
\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(g)^{m}\circ\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}}
for every positive integer
m

and thus Proposition
10.15
yields the desired principle

\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(g+1)\circ\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}}
.
∎

Lemma 10.17
.

For every integer
g\geq 2
the principle
\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(g)}
holds.

Proof.

Referring to Lemma
10.13
as a base case we argue by induction on
g
.
In the induction step we suppose that
g\geq 2
denotes an integer such
that
\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(g)}
is true. Repeated applications of the previous lemma disclose

\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(g)^{m}}
for every positive integer
m
and appealing once more to
Proposition
10.15
, this time with the empty sequence,
we infer
\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(g+1)}
. ∎

It should be clear that the two foregoing lemmata suffice for proving the following
statement by induction on
|\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}|
.

Corollary 10.18
.

For every sequence
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}\in\mathfrak{M}_{\leq}^{\times}
the principle

\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}}
is valid. ∎

Moreover, when unravelling the meaning of Lemma
10.17
one arrives
at a fairly strong form of the girth Ramsey theorem first announced
in §
4.4
.

Theorem 10.19
.

For every integer
g\geq 2
there exists a Ramsey construction

\Omega^{(g)}
that given an ordered
f
-partite hypergraph
F

with
\mathrm{girth}(F)>g
and a number of colours
r
produces an ordered

f
-partite system
\Omega^{(g)}_{r}(F)=(H,\mathscr{H})
satisfying

\mathscr{H}\longrightarrow(F)_{r}
and
\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{H}^{+})>g
.

Proof.

Let
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}=(F,\equiv^{F}_{0},\equiv^{F}_{1})
be the ordered
f
-partite
quasitrain associated to
F
(as in Example
10.2
).
We can view

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle F\hfil

as a train with parameter
(I)
, where
I
denotes
the domain of
f
. Since
\mathfrak{girth}(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}})>(g)
, the principle
\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(g)}

yields a train system
(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}},\mathscr{H})
such that
\mathscr{H}\longrightarrow(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}})_{r}

and
\mathfrak{Girth}(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}},\mathscr{H}^{+})>(g)
. Writing
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}=(H,\equiv^{H}_{0},\equiv^{H}_{1})

it remains to observe that
\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv^{H}_{0},\mathscr{H}^{+})>g

implies
\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{H}^{+})>g
(see Lemma
8.18
).
∎

In analogy to Lemma
3.18
we could add that the construction

\Omega^{(g)}
also preserves being
A
-intersecting, but due to a lack
of known applications we do not state this more carefully here.
Let us finally recall that every
k
-uniform hypergraph
F
can be viewed
as an
f
-partite hypergraph, where
f
denotes any function from a one-element
set to
\{k\}
. Therefore, Theorem
10.19
immediately yields a
Ramsey theorem for arbitrary hypergraphs without short cycles. As the
conclusion
\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{H}^{+})>g
implies
\mathrm{girth}(H)>g
(see Lemma
4.12
)
we thereby see that Theorem
10.19
yields Theorem
1.4
.
Let us collect all these implications into a single statement.

Summary 10.20
.

The conjunction of Proposition
10.14
and Proposition
10.15

leads to Corollary
10.18
, Theorem
10.19
, and to the girth
Ramsey theorem as formulated in Theorem
1.4
.

Remark 10.21
.

With the help of ordinal numbers our induction scheme can be reformulated
in a, perhaps, more transparent way.
The map
\varphi\colon\mathfrak{M}_{\leq}\longrightarrow\omega^{\omega}
defined by

\varphi(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})=\omega^{g_{m}-2}+\dots+\omega^{g_{1}-2}

is bijective. Thus Corollary
10.18
asserts
that
\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{\varphi^{-1}(\alpha)}
holds for every positive
ordinal
\alpha
beneath
\omega^{\omega}
. The proof is by induction
on
\alpha
, its base case
\alpha=1
agrees with Lemma
10.13
,
and Proposition
10.14
takes care of the successor step

\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{\varphi^{-1}(\alpha)}\Longrightarrow\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{\varphi^{-1}(\alpha+1)}
.
Finally, Proposition
10.15
provides the limit step, for in the
notation employed there
the sequence
\langle\varphi((g)^{m}\circ\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}})\colon m<\omega\rangle

converges to the limit number
