.

11.
Trains in the extension process

In this section we take the first major step towards proving
Proposition
10.14
. Notice that we are given there
a construction applicable to certain trains of height
m=|\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}|
,
and we are to exhibit another construction capable of handling certain
trains of height
m+1
. The plan for accomplishing this height increment
is to use the extension process; the main result of this section describes
how far we can go with this idea (see Lemma
11.10
). The main deficit
of the construction we obtain is that the copies it produces can still intersect
in entire
1
-wagons.
Following the arguments we saw in §
9.3
this can be remedied
by means of the partite construction method, but we defer the details of this
cleaning step to §
12.4
.

11.1.

The extension process discussed in Section
6
generalises
from pretrains to quasitrains of arbitrary height and our next immediate goal
is to develop an appropriate language for the description of such constructions.
In other words, we repeat §

in a more intricate setting.

In general,

-extensions of trains are only known to be quasitrains, but they
may fail to be trains. This is for the reason that two edges of an enlarged

-wagon

actually, this is the only obstacle.

\{\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}_{j}\colon j\in J\}
is a family of mutually
vertex-disjoint
f
-partite quasitrains of the same height
m\in{\mathds{N}}
,
say
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}_{j}=(G_{j},\equiv^{j}_{0},\ldots,\equiv^{j}_{m})
for every
j\in J
.
By the
union
of this family we mean the
f
-partite quasitrain

\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}=(G,\equiv^{G}_{0},\ldots,\equiv^{G}_{m})
with

V(G)=\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits_{j\in J}V(G_{j})\quad\text{ and }\quad E(G)=\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits_{j\in J}E(G_{j})

whose equivalence relations are defined as follows.

\bullet

If
e^{\prime},e^{\prime\prime}\in E(G)
and
\mu\in[0,m)
, then
e^{\prime}\equiv^{G}_{\mu}e^{\prime\prime}

means that there is an index
j\in J
with
e^{\prime},e^{\prime\prime}\in E(G_{j})

and
e^{\prime}\equiv^{j}_{\mu}e^{\prime\prime}
.

\bullet

Moreover,
e^{\prime}\equiv^{G}_{m}e^{\prime\prime}
holds for all edges
e^{\prime},e^{\prime\prime}\in E(G)
.

One checks immediately that

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle G\hfil

is indeed a quasitrain of height
m
and
that
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}_{j}
is a subquasitrain of

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle G\hfil

for every
j\in J
. If the
quasitrains
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}_{j}
are ordered, we order the vertex classes of

\hfil\textstyle G\hfil

in such a

Proof.

Writing
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}=(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})
we shall prove first

(11.2)

\mathfrak{Girth}(P,\equiv^{P}_{\mu-1},\mathscr{P}^{+})>g_{\mu}\quad\text{ for every $\mu\in[m]$.}

To this end we recall that Lemma
10.8

tells us
\mathfrak{girth}(F,\equiv^{F}_{\mu-1})>g_{\mu}
,
which due to Lemma
8.17
implies

\mathfrak{Girth}\bigl(F,\equiv^{F}_{\mu-1},E^{+}(F)\cup\{(F,\equiv^{F}_{\mu-1})\}\bigr)>g_{\mu}
.
Since big cycles of the pretrain system
(P,\equiv^{P}_{\mu-1},\mathscr{P}^{+})
cannot
jump from one copy in
\mathscr{P}
to another copy, this confirms (
11.2
).

Moreover, Lemma
8.11
immediately implies
\mathfrak{Girth}(P,\equiv^{P}_{m},\mathscr{P}^{+})>1
.
∎

We proceed with a full description as to how this construction

\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle G\hfil$\crcr}}}_{\star}
, while for
\mu\in[m]
the
\mu
-wagons of
these trains “remain separate from each other”.

Later we will need to know that

(11.5)

if
F_{\star}\in\mathscr{S}_{G}
and
x
is an isolated vertex of
F_{\star}
,
then
x
is isolated in
G
.

Indeed, by the definition of wagon assimilation,
x
is also isolated
in
\widehat{F}
and thus in every member of
\mathfrak{G}
.

We proceed by discussing the hypergraphs
H
and
N
.
Clearly,
H
is living in
N
(cf. Step
(0 )
) and the
system derived from
\mathscr{N}
is
\mathscr{H}_{\bullet}
(cf. Step
(0 )
).
By Step
(0 )
the copies in
\mathscr{N}
are strongly induced and, therefore, Fact
9.4
tells us that the system
(H,\mathscr{H}_{\bullet})
has strongly
induced copies, too.
Together with (
11.3
) and the fact that strong inducedness
is a transitive relation this proves
( )
‣
11.2
.

Let us now write
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}=(g_{1},\dots,g_{m})
and fix some
\mu\in[m]
.
Due to

(11.6)

\mathfrak{Girth}(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle N\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle N\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle N\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle N\hfil$\crcr}}},\mathscr{N}^{+})>\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}

we know
\mathfrak{Girth}(N,\equiv^{N}_{\mu-1},\mathscr{N}^{+})>g_{\mu}
.
As the pretrain
(H,\equiv^{H}_{\mu})
is derived from
(N,\equiv^{N}_{\mu-1})

(cf. Step
(0 )
), Lemma
9.6
translates this to

\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv^{H}_{\mu},\mathscr{H}^{+}_{\bullet})>g_{\mu}
, which together
with (
11.4
) and Lemma
9.12
reveals

\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv^{H}_{\mu},\mathscr{H}^{+})>g_{\mu}
.

So in order to establish
( )
‣
11.2
it only remains to
prove
\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv^{H}_{m+1},\mathscr{H}^{+})>1
.
The related statement

(11.7)

\mathfrak{Girth}(H,\equiv^{H}_{m+1},\mathscr{H}^{+}_{\bullet})>1

can be shown as in the previous paragraph by observing that (
11.6
)
contains the information
\mathfrak{Girth}(N,\equiv^{N}_{m},\mathscr{N}^{+})>1
and invoking
Lemma
9.6
.

Now let
F_{1},F_{2}\in\mathscr{H}^{+}
be two distinct copies having a
vertex
x
in common. According to Lemma
8.11
and symmetry it
suffices to exhibit an edge
e\in E(F_{1})
such that
x\in e
. Assume contrariwise
that
x
is an isolated vertex of
F_{1}
.

In particular,
F_{1}
is a real copy. Let
G_{1}\in\mathscr{H}_{\bullet}
be
the copy one of whose standard copies is
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}_{1}
.
If
F_{2}
is a real copy as well
we determine
G_{2}\in\mathscr{H}_{\bullet}
similarly
and if
F_{2}
is an edge copy we set
G_{2}=F_{2}
.

Due to (
11.5
) we know that
x
is isolated in
G_{1}
.
Moreover, the copies
G_{1},G_{2}\in\mathscr{H}^{+}_{\bullet}
have the vertex
x

in common. If they were distinct, then (
11.7
) and Lemma
8.11

would lead to the contradiction that
x
is non-isolated in
G_{1}
.

So altogether
G_{1}=G_{2}\in\mathscr{H}_{\bullet}
is a real copy and,
therefore,
F_{1}
and
F_{2}
are two distinct standard copies
in
G_{1}
. But now
x\in V(F_{1})\cap V(F_{2})
contradicts
F_{1}\neq F_{2}

because of the construction of

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle G\hfil

.
∎

12.
Trains in partite constructions

In this section we complete the proof of Proposition
10.14

and establish Proposition
10.15
. Both tasks are accomplished
by means of the partite construction method and thus we begin with
some general remarks on train pictures.

12.1.
Quasitrain constructions

Since it allows us to ignore parameters, it will be easier to study
quasitrains in partite constructions first.
Suppose that
\Phi
denotes a Ramsey construction for hypergraphs and that
\Xi

is a partite lemma applicable to
k
-partite
k
-uniform quasitrains of a
fixed height
m\in{\mathds{N}}
. As we shall see below, we can then define a
construction
\mathrm{PC}(\Phi,\Xi)
applicable to quasitrains of height
m
.

Let us first introduce some terminology for such situations.
Suppose that
(G,\mathscr{G})
is a system of hypergraphs,
where

endowed with a fixed quasitrain structure

12.2.
Train amalgamations

The next problem is whether the partite construction method can handle trains
instead of quasitrains as well. That is, we shall need to know
suitable conditions on constructions
\Phi
,
\Xi
, and trains

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle F\hfil

guaranteeing that for every number of colours
r
the quasitrain

\mathrm{PC}(\Phi,\Xi)_{r}(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}})
turns out to be a train.
As usual, our strategy is to enforce that all quasitrain pictures

(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle\Pi\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle\Pi\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle\Pi\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle\Pi\hfil$\crcr}}},\mathscr{P},\psi)
generated along the way have the property
that their underlying quasitrains

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

are trains. This is already somewhat problematic for

and not just a hypergraph system. We are thus led to the following notion of train

Proof.

Recall that the
f
-partite structure of
\Pi
is defined
by
V_{i}(\Pi)=\psi^{-1}\bigl(V_{i}(G)\bigr)
for every index

in the domain of

Thus the sets
D_{\mu}=e\cap V_{A_{\mu}}(G)
satisfy

V_{D_{\mu}}(\Pi^{e})=\psi^{-1}(D_{\mu})=\psi^{-1}(e)\cap\psi^{-1}\bigl(V_{A_{\mu}}(G)\bigr)=V(\Pi^{e})\cap V_{A_{\mu}}(\Pi)

for every
\mu\in[m]
.

Now if two edges
e_{\star}
,
e_{\star\star}\in E(\Pi^{e})

belong to the same
\mu

(\mu-1)
-wagon
of

e_{\star}\cap e_{\star\star}\subseteq V(\Pi^{e})\cap V_{A_{\mu}}(\Pi)=V_{D_{\mu}}(\Pi^{e})

∎

When executing partite constructions with train pictures, we can maintain parameters
by appealing to the following result.

Lemma 12.3

the

assumptions mean

)

(

)

(

for

Due to Lemma

and
(0 )

To this end we consider a big cycle

in

m

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle\Sigma\hfil

Due to Lemma
8.11

passing through

.

If

we denote the standard copy of

to which

belongs by
(\Pi_{1},\mathscr{P}_{1}^{+})
and we let

be the copy extended by
\Pi_{1}
. If, on the other hand,

, then we set
\Pi^{e}_{1}=F_{1}
. So in both cases we

. Let
\Pi_{2}^{e}
be defined similarly with respect to

.

If

, then
F_{1}
,
F_{2}
belong to a common standard copy
and the existence of

follows from
(0 )
.
So we can henceforth assume
\Pi^{e}_{1}\neq\Pi^{e}_{2}
. Since
\mathscr{C}
is a big cycle,
each of the copies
F_{1}
,

has at least one edge, and

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle H\hfil

we can thus form a big cycle

. Owing to

and Lemma

there exists an

In the special case

of

\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}\in\mathfrak{M}^{\times}
there exists a Ramsey construction
for

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle g\hfil

-trains.

Proof.

Due to Lemma
10.13
and Proposition
10.14
we have

\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(2)^{m}}
for every positive integer
m
. Clearly, every construction
exemplifying
\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(2)^{m}}
for
m=|\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}|
is a Ramsey construction

∎

Proof.

We keep using the notation from Definition
12.9
and (

).
As a first step we shall show that

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle A\hfil

parametrises

\textstyle\relbar

\textstyle\rightharpoonup

\hfil\textstyle H\hfil

.
Due to
\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(g)^{m}\circ\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}}
the train

\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle H\hfil$\crcr}}}_{\bullet}=(H,\equiv_{0}^{H},\sim_{1}^{H},\dots,\sim_{m-1}^{H},\equiv_{1}^{H},\ldots,\equiv_{\ell+1}^{H})

has the same parameter as
\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}_{\bullet}
, i.e.,

\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle B\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle B\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle B\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle B\hfil$\crcr}}}\circ(A_{2},\dots,A_{\ell+1})

Setting for simplicity
\sim^{H}_{0}=\equiv^{H}_{0}
and
\sim^{H}_{m}=\equiv^{H}_{1}
this means
that for any two edges
e,e^{\prime}\in E(H)
the following two statements hold.

(
0
)

If
\mu\in[m]
,
e\sim^{H}_{\mu}e^{\prime}
,
and
e\not\sim^{H}_{\mu-1}e^{\prime}
, then
e\cap e^{\prime}\subseteq V_{B_{\mu}}(H)
.

(
0
)

If
\lambda\in[2,\ell+1]
,
e\equiv^{H}_{\lambda}e^{\prime}
,
and
e\not\equiv^{H}_{\lambda-1}e^{\prime}
,
then
e\cap e^{\prime}\subseteq V_{A_{\lambda}}(H)
.

In view of
(0 )
it only remains to be shown that all
edges
e,e^{\prime}\in E(H)
with
e\equiv^{H}_{1}e^{\prime}
and
e\not\equiv^{H}_{0}e^{\prime}

satisfy
e\cap e^{\prime}\subseteq V_{A_{1}}(H)
. Due to
e\sim^{H}_{m}e^{\prime}
there
exists a smallest integer
\mu\in[0,m]
such that
e\sim^{H}_{\mu}e^{\prime}
.
Since
e\not\sim^{H}_{0}e^{\prime}
, we have
\mu>0
, and thus the minimality of
\mu

yields
e\not\sim^{H}_{\mu-1}e^{\prime}
. So
(0 )

reveals
e\cap e^{\prime}\subseteq V_{B_{\mu}}(H)
and because of
B_{\mu}\subseteq A_{1}

the desired inclusion
e\cap e^{\prime}\subseteq V_{A_{1}}(H)
follows.

. As the train construction
\Psi^{m}

exemplifies the principle

,
the partition relation
\mathscr{H}\longrightarrow(\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle F\hfil$\crcr}}})_{r}

i.e., the conversion of the given

-principles

\textstyle\relbar

12.6.
Train constituents

Recall that our initial motivation for introducing trains was the observation
that partite constructions produce trains; moreover trains seem to offer a
chance to handle hypergraphs of the next larger girth in the context of an
argument by induction. In some sense, this
subsection is the place of the whole article where all these hopes materialise.

Lemma 12.13
.

There exists a
((g+1)\circ\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}})
-amenable partite lemma
\Xi
.

This partite lemma
\Xi
will be obtained by a diagonal variation
of the partite construction method. Vertically we use an arbitrary
Ramsey construction
\Phi
for
((g+1)\circ\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}})
-trains
(see Corollary
12.8
). Horizontally the basic observation is that
it was never written into stone that one has to employ the very same
partite lemma in each stage of the iterative procedure.
Rather, it is reasonable to adjust to the increasing complexity
of the arising pictures by using more and more sophisticated partite lemmata
as the construction progresses.
In fact, we plan to use
\Psi^{m}
when we need a partite lemma
for the
m^{\mathrm{th}}
time,
so a suggestive notation for the construction we are about to describe
could be

\Xi=\mathrm{PC}\bigl(\Phi,(\Psi^{m})_{m\in{\mathds{N}}}\bigr)
.
Here is the picturesque statement we shall iterate.

is
((g+1)\circ\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}})
-amenable. ∎

It is now immediate from Lemma
12.6
that the construction

\mathrm{PC}(\Phi,\Xi)
, where
\Phi
again denotes a Ramsey construction for

((g+1)\circ\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}})
-trains, exemplifies
\scalebox{1.2}[1.2]{{$\diamondsuit$}}_{(g+1)\circ\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\displaystyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\textstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.8mu\leaders{\hbox{$\smash{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\relbar$}}\mkern-4.0mu$}}{\hfill}\raisebox{0.0pt}[2.0pt][1.0pt]{\scalebox{0.55}{$\scriptscriptstyle\rightharpoonup$}}\mkern 0.8mu$\crcr\kern-1.0pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle g\hfil$\crcr}}}}
.
This concludes the proof of Proposition
10.15
.
In the light of our earlier work
Corollary
10.18
, Theorem
10.19
, and
Theorem
1.4
have thereby been demonstrated as well (see Summary
10.20
).

13.
Paradise

This section is concerned with the proofs of
Theorem
1.7
and Theorem
1.6
. To this end we need
a connection between
\mathrm{Girth}
and forests of copies, which is established
in §
13.1
. The main result there (Lemma
13.11
)
asserts that large
\mathrm{Girth}
forces small sets of copies to be forests.
In §
13.2
this lemma will allow us to analyse a partite
construction utilising the construction
\Omega^{(g)}
provided by Theorem
10.19

as a partite lemma. As a result, we shall prove Theorem
1.7
in a very
strong form (Theorem
13.12
).
The deduction of Theorem
1.6
will then be straightforward.

13.1.
Forests of copies

Let us recall that forests of copies were introduced in Definition
1.5

as being certain systems
\mathscr{N}\subseteq\binom{H}{F}
consisting of mutually
isomorphic copies.

Marginally generalising the underlying setup, we shall henceforth say for a linear system
of hypergraphs
(H,\mathscr{N})
that
\mathscr{N}
is a
forest of copies

if one can write
\mathscr{N}=\{F_{1},\ldots,F_{|\mathscr{N}|}\}
in such a way that
for every
j\in[2,|\mathscr{N}|]
the set

z_{j}=V(F_{j})\cap\bigl(\bigcup_{i<j}V(F_{i})\bigr)
is either an edge
in
E(F_{j})\cap\bigl(\bigcup_{i<j}E(F_{i})\bigr)
or it consists of at most
one vertex.

In this situation,
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{|\mathscr{N}|})

is called an
admissible enumeration
of
\mathscr{N}
.

It may be helpful to point out that forests of copies are thereby allowed
to contain both edge copies and real copies.

Most results in this subsection can be regarded as appropriate adaptations
of well-known facts on ordinary forests—a notion briefly recapitulated immediately
before Theorem
1.1
. To distinguish such forests from forests of copies we shall
call them
edge forests
in the discussion that follows.

Here is a list of four standard facts on edge forests.

(

)

Every subset of an edge forest is again an edge forest.

(

)

The result of gluing two edge forests together along a
vertex or an edge is again an edge forest.

(

)

If a hypergraph
H=(V,E)
satisfies
\mathrm{girth}(H)>|E|
, then

E
is an edge forest.

(

)

Every edge forest consisting of at least two edges has
at least two leaves (belonging to different edges).

Now we already saw in the introduction that forests of copies are not closed
under taking subsets, meaning that the naïve generalisation of
( )
‣
13.1
fails
(see Figure
1.1
).
Nevertheless, we shall show in Lemma
13.4
that deleting edge copies preserves
being a forest of copies. In Lemma
13.5
and Lemma
13.6
we shall
then see that
( )
‣
13.1
generalises in the obvious way.
Statement
( )
‣
13.1
remains valid if we replace lower case
\mathrm{girth}
by
capital
\mathrm{Girth}
(see Lemma
13.11
). Finally, when dealing
with
( )
‣
13.1
we shall work with the following analogue of edges acting as “leaves”.

Definition 13.1
.

Given a forest of copies
\mathscr{N}
and a copy
F_{\star}\in\mathscr{N}
we say that
F_{\star}

is
terminal in
\mathscr{N}
if there exists an admissible enumeration

(F_{1},\ldots,F_{|\mathscr{N}|})
of
\mathscr{N}
such that
F_{\star}=F_{|\mathscr{N}|}
.

For instance, if
\mathscr{N}
denotes a forest consisting of two copies, then both enumerations
of
\mathscr{N}
are admissible and, consequently, both copies in
\mathscr{N}
are terminal.
Now the variant of
( )
‣
13.1
we have been alluding to reads as follows.

Lemma 13.2
.

Every forest of at least two copies possesses at least two terminal copies.

In the argument that follows and at several other occasions occurring in the rest of
this section it will be convenient to employ the following notation. Given a set of
hypergraphs
\mathscr{N}
, we shall write
V(\mathscr{N})
for
\bigcup_{F_{\star}\in\mathscr{N}}V(F_{\star})

and, similarly,
E(\mathscr{N})
will abbreviate
\bigcup_{F_{\star}\in\mathscr{N}}E(F_{\star})
.

Proof of Lemma
13.2
.

We argue by induction on the size
|\mathscr{N}|
of the forest of copies
under consideration. The base case
|\mathscr{N}|=2
has already been studied.
For the induction step we suppose that
\mathscr{N}

is a forest consisting of
n\geq 3
copies and that every forest
of copies
\mathscr{N}^{\prime}
with
|\mathscr{N}^{\prime}|=n-1
has at least two terminal copies.

Since
\mathscr{N}
admits an admissible enumeration, it possesses some terminal
copy
F_{\star}
. Notice that the
set

z_{\star}=V(F_{\star})\cap V(\mathscr{N}\smallsetminus\{F_{\star}\})

is either an edge in
E(F_{\star})\cap E(\mathscr{N}\smallsetminus\{F_{\star}\})

or it consists of at most one vertex. Therefore there exists a copy

F_{\circ}\in\mathscr{N}\smallsetminus\{F_{\star}\}
such that

\bullet

z_{\star}\subseteq V(F_{\circ})

\bullet

and if
z_{\star}
is an edge, then
z_{\star}\in E(F_{\circ})
.

The terminality of
F_{\star}
implies that
\mathscr{N}\smallsetminus\{F_{\star}\}
is a forest
of copies and the induction hypothesis yields an admissible
enumeration
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n-1})
of
\mathscr{N}\smallsetminus\{F_{\star}\}

whose terminal copy is distinct from
F_{\circ}
. We contend that
F_{n-1}

is terminal in
\mathscr{N}
as well and that the enumeration

(13.1)

(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n-2},F_{\star},F_{n-1})

exemplifies this fact. The claims that we need to check concerning the
copies
F_{2},\ldots,F_{n-2}
follow immediately
from the admissibility of
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n-1})
, and the claim
on
F_{\star}
is a consequence of
F_{\circ}\in\{F_{1},\ldots,F_{n-2}\}
.
It remains to verify that the set

z^{+}=V(F_{n-1})\cap V\bigl(\{F_{1},\ldots,F_{n-2},F_{\star}\}\bigr)

is either an edge
in
E(F_{n-1})\cap E\bigl(\{F_{1},\ldots,F_{n-2},F_{\star}\}\bigr)
or that it
consists of at most one vertex.
Due to the admissibility of
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n-1})
we know that
the set

z^{-}=V(F_{n-1})\cap V\bigl(\{F_{1},\ldots,F_{n-2}\}\bigr)

has analogous properties and thus it suffices to prove
z^{+}=z^{-}
.
Because of

V(F_{n-1})\cap V(F_{\star})\subseteq V(F_{n-1})\cap z_{\star}\subseteq V(F_{n-1})\cap V(F_{\circ})\subseteq z^{-}

and

z^{+}=z^{-}\cup\bigl(V(F_{n-1})\cap V(F_{\star})\bigr)

this is indeed the case.
Altogether we have thereby proved that the enumeration (
13.1
) is
admissible. Hence
F_{\star}
and
F_{n-1}
are two terminal copies of
\mathscr{N}
,
and the induction step is complete.
∎

The concept “dual” to a terminal copy is that of an
initial copy
,
by which we mean a copy in a forest that is capable of standing in the first position
of an admissible enumeration.

Lemma 13.3
.

In a forest of copies every copy is initial.

Proof.

Again we argue by induction on the size of the forest under consideration.
In the base case, when the forest consists of at most two copies, every
enumeration is admissible and, therefore, every copy is initial.

For the induction step we look at a forest of copies
\mathscr{N}

with
n=|\mathscr{N}|\geq 3
and at an arbitrary copy
F_{1}\in\mathscr{N}
.
Lemma
13.2

discloses that
\mathscr{N}
has a terminal copy
F_{n}\neq F_{1}
.
Now
\mathscr{N}^{\prime}=\mathscr{N}\smallsetminus\{F_{n}\}
is again a forest of copies and due to the
induction hypothesis
F_{1}
is an initial copy of
\mathscr{N}^{\prime}
, i.e., there is
an admissible enumeration
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n-1})
of
\mathscr{N}^{\prime}
that starts
with
F_{1}
. Clearly
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n})
is an admissible enumeration
of
\mathscr{N}
and, consequently,
F_{1}
is indeed an initial copy of
\mathscr{N}
.
∎

Next we address “subforests” of copies obtained by the removal of edge copies.

Lemma 13.4
.

The result of deleting an edge copy from a forest of copies is again
a forest of copies.

Proof.

Let
\mathscr{N}
be a forest of copies containing some edge copy
e^{+}
.
We are to prove that
\mathscr{N}^{\prime}=\mathscr{N}\smallsetminus\{e^{+}\}
is a forest of copies as well.
To avoid trivialities we may suppose that
\mathscr{N}^{\prime}\neq\varnothing
. If
e\in E(\mathscr{N}^{\prime})

we choose a copy
F_{1}\in\mathscr{N}^{\prime}
satisfying
e\in E(F_{1})
and otherwise we
let
F_{1}\in\mathscr{N}^{\prime}
be arbitrary. By Lemma
13.3
there is
an admissible enumeration

(F_{1},\ldots,F_{i},e^{+},F_{i+1},\ldots,F_{|\mathscr{N}^{\prime}|})

of
\mathscr{N}
starting with
F_{1}
and one checks immediately that
the enumeration
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{|\mathscr{N}^{\prime}|})
of
\mathscr{N}^{\prime}
obtained by deleting
e^{+}

is admissible.
∎

Roughly speaking, the lemma that follows asserts that if we glue two forests
of copies
\mathscr{A}
and
\mathscr{B}
together at a vertex, then the result is again
a forest of copies.

Lemma 13.5
.

Suppose that
(H,\mathscr{N})
is a linear system of hypergraphs admitting a
partition
\mathscr{N}=\mathscr{A}\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\mathscr{B}
such that

|V(\mathscr{A})\cap V(\mathscr{B})|\leq 1
.
If both
\mathscr{A}
and
\mathscr{B}
are forests of copies, then so is
\mathscr{N}
.

Proof.

The case
\mathscr{B}=\varnothing
being clear we may suppose that
\mathscr{B}
contains at least
one copy. Since the set
z=V(\mathscr{A})\cap V(\mathscr{B})
consists of at most one vertex,
there exists a copy
F^{\prime}_{1}\in\mathscr{B}
such that
z\subseteq V(F^{\prime}_{1})
. Now
Lemma
13.3
shows that
\mathscr{B}
has an admissible
enumeration
(F^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,F^{\prime}_{|\mathscr{B}|})
starting with
F^{\prime}_{1}
.
It is not hard to check that if
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{|\mathscr{A}|})
is an arbitrary
admissible enumeration of
\mathscr{A}
, then the enumeration

(F_{1},\ldots,F_{|\mathscr{A}|},F^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,F^{\prime}_{|\mathscr{B}|})
of
\mathscr{N}
is admissible
as well.
∎

There is a similar statement addressing the case that the glueing occurs
in an entire edge of the underlying hypergraph.

Lemma 13.6
.

Let
(H,\mathscr{N})
be a linear system of hypergraphs and let

\mathscr{N}=\mathscr{A}\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\cup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\mathscr{B}
be a partition such that
V(\mathscr{A})\cap V(\mathscr{B})\subseteq e

holds for some edge
e
of
H
.
If both
\mathscr{A}\cup\{e^{+}\}
and
\mathscr{B}\cup\{e^{+}\}
are forests of copies,
then so is
\mathscr{N}
.

Proof.

Take an arbitrary admissible enumeration
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{a})
of
\mathscr{A}\cup\{e^{+}\}
,
as well as an admissible enumeration
(e^{+},F^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,F^{\prime}_{b})
of
\mathscr{B}\cup\{e^{+}\}
,
where
a=|\mathscr{A}\cup\{e^{+}\}|
and
b=|\mathscr{B}\cup\{e^{+}\}|
, respectively.
Now
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{a},F^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,F^{\prime}_{b})
is an admissible enumeration
of
\mathscr{N}\cup\{e^{+}\}
. If
e^{+}\in\mathscr{N}
this proves that
\mathscr{N}
is indeed
a forest of copies and in case
e^{+}\not\in\mathscr{N}
Lemma
13.4
leads us to the
same conclusion.
∎

An iterative application of the next result will allow us to relate
forests of copies to
\mathrm{Girth}
.

Lemma 13.7
.

Given a linear system of hypergraphs
(H,\mathscr{N})

with
{\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{N}^{+})>|\mathscr{N}|\geq 2}
there exists a copy
F_{\star}\in\mathscr{N}

such that the set

(13.2)

z_{\star}=V(F_{\star})\cap V(\mathscr{N}\smallsetminus\{F_{\star}\})

is either an edge in
E(F_{\star})\cap E(\mathscr{N}\smallsetminus\{F_{\star}\})

or it consists of at most one vertex.

Proof.

Assume for the sake of contradiction that no such copy
F_{\star}
exists.
We aim at building a tidy cycle of copies in
(H,\mathscr{N}^{+})
consisting
of at most
|\mathscr{N}|
distinct copies, which does not possess a master copy.
Looking at the
potential connectors of such a cycle, we call a vertex
x\in V(H)

useful
if there exist distinct copies
F^{\prime},F^{\prime\prime}\in\mathscr{N}
such that

x\in V(F^{\prime})\cap V(F^{\prime\prime})
.
Similarly, an edge
e\in E(H)
is said to be

useful
if there are distinct copies
F^{\prime},F^{\prime\prime}\in\mathscr{N}
satisfying

e\in E(F^{\prime})\cap E(F^{\prime\prime})
.
For instance, for every copy
F_{\star}\in\mathscr{N}
all vertices belonging to the
corresponding set
z_{\star}
defined in (
13.2
) are useful.

Claim 13.8
.

For every useful vertex
x
there are two distinct copies
F^{\prime}_{x},F^{\prime\prime}_{x}\in\mathscr{N}

such that

(

)

x\in V(F^{\prime}_{x})\cap V(F^{\prime\prime}_{x})
;

(

)

and each of
F^{\prime}_{x}
,
F^{\prime\prime}_{x}
has at most one
useful edge containing
x
.

Proof.

Given
x
we consider an auxiliary set system
S_{x}
with vertex set

V(S_{x})=\bigl\{F_{\star}\in\mathscr{N}\colon x\in V(F_{\star})\bigr\}\,.

For every useful edge
e
containing
x
the set

\varphi_{e}=\bigl\{F_{\star}\in V(S_{x})\colon e\in E(F_{\star})\bigr\}

has at least the size
2
. Thus we can define the edge set of our set system
S_{x}

by

E(S_{x})=\bigl\{\varphi_{e}\colon\text{$e$ is useful and $x\in e$}\bigr\}\,.

We are to prove that
S_{x}
has at least two vertices whose degree
is at most one. Due to
v(S_{x})\geq 2
the failure of this statement would imply
that
S_{x}
contains some cycle
\varphi_{e(1)}F_{1}\ldots\varphi_{e(n)}F_{n}
(in the
sense of Definition
1.3
). But then
F_{1}e(2)\ldots F_{n}e(1)

is a tidy cycle of copies in
(H,\mathscr{N})
all of whose connectors are edges,
which in view of

\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{N}^{+})>|\mathscr{N}|\geq v(S_{x})\geq n

contradicts Lemma
4.15
.
∎

Next we shall construct a cycle of copies in
(H,\mathscr{N})
which has only vertex
connectors and some further special property.
We commence by examining desirable subsequences
of the form
q^{\prime}F_{\star}q^{\prime\prime}
of the envisaged cycle.
Given a copy
F_{\star}\in\mathscr{N}
and distinct useful vertices

q^{\prime},q^{\prime\prime}\in V(F_{\star})

we say that
F_{\star}
is secure between
q^{\prime}
and
q^{\prime\prime}
provided
the following statement holds: If there is an edge
f

satisfying
q^{\prime},q^{\prime\prime}\in f\in E(F_{\star})
, then this edge is not useful.
The intuition here is that it is impossible to collapse copies
that occur securely between their neighbouring connectors.

Claim 13.9
.

If
F_{\star}\in\mathscr{N}
and
q^{\prime}\in V(F_{\star})
is useful,
then there exists a copy
F_{\star\star}\in\mathscr{N}\smallsetminus\{F_{\star}\}
satisfying

q^{\prime}\in V(F_{\star\star})
together with another useful vertex

q^{\prime\prime}\in V(F_{\star\star})
such that

F_{\star\star}
is secure between
q^{\prime}
and
q^{\prime\prime}
.

Proof.

Let
F^{\prime}_{q^{\prime}},F^{\prime\prime}_{q^{\prime}}\in\mathscr{N}
be the copies Claim
13.8
provides
for
x=q^{\prime}
, choose

Let us call a cycle of copies
F_{1}q_{1}\ldots F_{n}q_{n}
in

(H,\mathscr{N})
or

\bullet

\bullet

and

Claim 13.10
.

There exist a special cycle of copies in
(H,\mathscr{N})
.

Proof.

An iterative application of Claim

allows us to

(

,

(
0
)

(
0
)

q_{i}
and

.

Indeed, let

be arbitrary and let

of our infinite sequence,

Since

such that

Thus if the connectors of

of copies.
∎

Throughout the rest of the proof we consider a special cycle of copies

Let us deal with case

Write

\displaystyle\mathscr{D}_{\mu}

Lemma 13.11
.

Let
(H,\mathscr{N})
be a linear system of hypergraphs.
If
\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{N}^{+})>|\mathscr{N}|
, then
\mathscr{N}
is a forest of copies.

Proof.

We argue by induction on
n=|\mathscr{N}|
, the base case
n=1
being clear.
In the induction step we have to deal with a linear system
(H,\mathscr{N})
consisting of
n\geq 2
copies that satisfies
\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{N}^{+})>|\mathscr{N}|
.
Let
F_{\star}\in\mathscr{N}
be a copy obtained by applying Lemma
13.7

to
\mathscr{N}
and set
\mathscr{N}_{\star}=\mathscr{N}\smallsetminus\{F_{\star}\}
.
Since
\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{N}_{\star}^{+})>|\mathscr{N}|>|\mathscr{N}_{\star}|
, the induction hypothesis
shows that
\mathscr{N}_{\star}
is a forest of copies. If
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n-1})

is an admissible enumeration of
\mathscr{N}_{\star}
,
then
(F_{1},\ldots,F_{n-1},F_{\star})
is the
desired admissible enumeration of
\mathscr{N}
.
∎

13.2.
The final partite construction

We shall prove the following strong form of
Theorem
1.7
alluded to in the introduction.

Theorem 13.12
.

Let a hypergraph
F
and a natural number
g\geq 2
satisfy

\mathrm{girth}(F)>g
. If
r,n\geq 2
are two further natural numbers, then there
exists a linear system of hypergraphs
(H,\mathscr{H})
such that

\bullet

\mathscr{H}\longrightarrow(F)_{r}

\bullet

and for every
\mathscr{N}\subseteq\mathscr{H}^{+}
with
|\mathscr{N}|\in[2,n]

there exists some
\mathscr{X}\subseteq\mathscr{H}

for which
\mathscr{N}\cup\mathscr{X}
is a forest of copies
and
|\mathscr{X}|\leq\frac{|\mathscr{N}|-2}{g-1}
.

Before we embark on the proof of this result we would like to point out
that for
n\leq g
it follows quickly from a pair of statements that have
been obtained earlier. Indeed, the construction
\Omega^{(g)}
(see
Theorem
10.19
) delivers a linear system of hypergraphs

(H,\mathscr{H})
such that
\mathscr{H}\longrightarrow(F)_{r}
and
\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{H}^{+})>g
.
Now for every
\mathscr{N}\subseteq\mathscr{H}^{+}
with
|\mathscr{N}|\in[2,g]
we have

\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{N}^{+})>g\geq|\mathscr{N}|
and owing to Lemma
13.11

this implies that
\mathscr{N}
is a forest of copies. In other words, the second
bullet holds for
\mathscr{X}=\varnothing
, as desired.

The general case of Theorem
13.12
will be proved by means of a
further application of the partite construction method. This will involve
pictures of the following kind.

Definition 13.13
.

Given integers
g,n\geq 2
a picture
(\Pi,\mathscr{P},\psi)
is said to be

(g,n)
-certified
if each of its constituents
\Pi^{e}
satisfies

\mathrm{girth}(\Pi^{e})>n
and for every
\mathscr{N}\subseteq\mathscr{P}^{+}
with
|\mathscr{N}|\in[2,n]

there exists some
\mathscr{X}\subseteq\mathscr{P}
such that
\mathscr{N}\cup\mathscr{X}
is a forest of
copies and
|\mathscr{X}|\leq\frac{|\mathscr{N}|-2}{g-1}
.

Let us show first that being certified is a property we can expect any reasonable
picture zero to have.

Lemma 13.14
.

Suppose that a hypergraph
F
and an integer
g\geq 2
satisfy
\mathrm{girth}(F)>g
.
If
(G,\mathscr{G})
denotes any linear system of hypergraphs
with
\mathscr{G}\subseteq\binom{G}{F}
, then the picture zero over this system
is
(g,n)
-certified for every integer
n\geq 2
.

Proof.

Let
(\Pi,\mathscr{P},\psi)
denote the picture zero under discussion. Since all of
its constituents are matchings, their girth is greater than
n
for every
n\geq 2
.
Proceeding with the second property, we suppose that
any
\mathscr{N}\subseteq\mathscr{P}^{+}
with
|\mathscr{N}|\geq 2
is given.
For every copy
F_{\star}\in\mathscr{P}
we set

\mathscr{N}(F_{\star})=\mathscr{N}\cap\bigl(E^{+}(F_{\star})\cup\{F_{\star}\}\bigr)
. Since
\Pi

is the disjoint union of the copies in
\mathscr{P}
, this stipulation yields
a partition
\mathscr{N}=\mathop{\vphantom{\bigcup}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr\bigcup\cr\cdot\crcr}}}}\displaylimits_{F_{\star}\in\mathscr{P}}\mathscr{N}(F_{\star})
.

There are two sufficient conditions ensuring that a partition class

\mathscr{N}(F_{\star})
is a forest of copies. First, if
F_{\star}\in N(F_{\star})
,
then every enumeration of
\mathscr{N}(F_{\star})
starting with
F_{\star}
itself
is admissible. Second, if
F_{\star}\not\in\mathscr{N}(F_{\star})
and
|\mathscr{N}(F_{\star})|\leq g
,
then
\mathscr{N}(F_{\star})
is a forest of edge copies due to
\mathrm{girth}(F_{\star})>g
.
For these reasons, the set

\mathscr{X}=\bigl\{F_{\star}\in\mathscr{P}\colon|\mathscr{N}(F_{\star})|\geq g+1\bigr\}

has the property that
\mathscr{N}\cup\mathscr{X}
is a forest of copies.

So it remains to prove
|\mathscr{X}|\leq\frac{|\mathscr{N}|-2}{g-1}
.
The obvious bound

rewrites as

(g-1)|\mathscr{X}|+2(|\mathscr{X}|-1)\leq|\mathscr{N}|-2

and provided that
\mathscr{X}
is nonempty the desired upper bound on
|\mathscr{X}|

follows. Moreover, if
\mathscr{X}
is empty, then we just need to appeal
to
|\mathscr{N}|\geq 2
.
∎

The picturesque lemma appropriate for the present context reads as follows.

Lemma 13.15

Suppose that
g,n\geq 2

(\Sigma,\mathscr{Q},\psi_{\Sigma})=(\Pi,\mathscr{P},\psi_{\Pi})\mathbin{\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\displaystyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\textstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}{\vtop{\halign{\hfil$\m@th\scriptscriptstyle#$\hfil\cr+\cr\times\crcr}}}}(H,\mathscr{H})

We shall say that

Arguing indirectly we fix a good pair

(
0
)

\big|\varphi[\mathscr{N}]\big|
minimal.

\text{$(\mathscr{A}^{\prime},\alpha)$ and $(\mathscr{B}^{\prime},\beta)$ are good pairs,

Next we seek to establish

For all these reasons

The demand

‣

follows from

\xi[\mathscr{X}]\subseteq\upsilon[\mathscr{Y}]\cup\zeta[\mathscr{Z}]\overset{\text{\ref{it:6149b}}}{\subseteq}\alpha[\mathscr{A}^{\prime}]\cup\beta[\mathscr{B}^{\prime}]\overset{\eqref{eq:6111}}{=}\varphi[\mathscr{A}]\cup\varphi[\mathscr{B}]=\varphi[\mathscr{N}]\,.

For the verification of
( )
‣
13.2
we want to apply Lemma
13.6

to
\mathscr{A}\cup\mathscr{Y}
,
\mathscr{B}\cup\mathscr{Z}
, and
x
here in place of
\mathscr{A}
,
\mathscr{B}
,
and
e
there. As the assumption that
(\mathscr{A}\cup\mathscr{Y})\cup\{x^{+}\}=\mathscr{A}^{\prime}\cup\mathscr{Y}

and
(\mathscr{B}\cup\mathscr{Z})\cup\{x^{+}\}=\mathscr{B}^{\prime}\cup\mathscr{Z}
need to be forests of copies
are satisfied by our choice of the good pairs
(\mathscr{Y},\upsilon)
and
(\mathscr{Z},\zeta)
,
it remains to check that

(13.10)

V(\mathscr{A}\cup\mathscr{Y})\cap V(\mathscr{B}\cup\mathscr{Z})\subseteq x\,.

Towards the proof of this inclusion we observe that

V(F_{\star})\cap V(H)\subseteq V\bigl(\varphi(F_{\star})\bigr)
holds for
every
F_{\star}\in\mathscr{A}
, whence
V(\mathscr{A})\cap V(H)\subseteq V(\varphi[\mathscr{A}])
.
Similarly one has

V(\mathscr{Y})\cap V(H)\subseteq V(\upsilon[\mathscr{Y}])\overset{\text{\ref{it:6149b}}}{\subseteq}V(\alpha[\mathscr{A}^{\prime}])\overset{\eqref{eq:6111}}{=}V(\varphi[\mathscr{A}])

and both statements together yield
V(\mathscr{A}\cup\mathscr{Y})\cap V(H)\subseteq V(\varphi[\mathscr{A}])
.
Proceeding similarly with
\mathscr{B}\cup\mathscr{Z}
and combining the results
we infer

(13.11)

\bigl(V(\mathscr{A}\cup\mathscr{Y})\cap V(\mathscr{B}\cup\mathscr{Z})\bigr)\cap V(H)\subseteq V(\varphi[\mathscr{A}])\cap V(\varphi[\mathscr{B}])=x\,.

Moreover, the definition of the partite amalgamation (
13.3
) entails
V(F_{\star})\cap V(F_{\star\star})\subseteq V(H)
for all
F_{\star}\in\mathscr{A}\cup\mathscr{Y}

and
F_{\star\star}\in\mathscr{B}\cup\mathscr{Z}
and for this reason
we have

V(\mathscr{A}\cup\mathscr{Y})\cap V(\mathscr{B}\cup\mathscr{Z})\subseteq V(H)\,.

Together with (
13.11
) this establishes (
13.10
) and thus
concludes the proof of (
13.9
).

However, in the light of

|\mathscr{X}|\leq|\mathscr{Y}|+|\mathscr{Z}|\overset{\eqref{eq:6141}}{\leq}\frac{|\mathscr{A}|-1}{g-1}+\frac{|\mathscr{B}|-1}{g-1}=\frac{|\mathscr{N}|-2}{g-1}

this contradicts
(0 )
. In other words, the case that
x
is an edge
is impossible.

Second Case.
|x|\leq 1
.

We argue similar as in the first case. The pairs
(\mathscr{A},\varphi\upharpoonright\mathscr{A})

and
(\mathscr{B},\varphi\upharpoonright\mathscr{B})
are good and the main point is that they
are resolved by certain good pairs
(\mathscr{Y},\upsilon)
and
(\mathscr{Z},\zeta)

such that

(13.12)

|\mathscr{Y}|\leq\frac{|\mathscr{A}|-1}{g-1}\quad\text{ and }\quad|\mathscr{Z}|\leq\frac{|\mathscr{B}|-1}{g-1}\,,

respectively. In fact, if
|\mathscr{A}|\geq 2
we can argue exactly as in the first
case in order to obtain such a good pair
(\mathscr{Y},\upsilon)
satisfying the
stronger estimate
|\mathscr{Y}|\leq\frac{|\mathscr{A}|-2}{g-1}
. Moreover, in case

|\mathscr{A}|=1
we can just take
\mathscr{Y}=\upsilon=\varnothing
.
The claim on
(\mathscr{Z},\zeta)
is proved in the same way.

Again we set
\mathscr{X}=\mathscr{Y}\cup\mathscr{Z}
and take a map
\xi\subseteq\upsilon\cup\zeta

from
\mathscr{X}
to
\mathscr{H}^{+}
.
We remark that (
13.10
) is still valid in the present case and the only
change we need to make when concluding that
\mathscr{N}\cup\mathscr{X}
is a forest of copies
is that this time we need to appeal to Lemma
13.5
. Apart from these
small modifications, the proof that the good pair
(\mathscr{X},\xi)

resolves
(\mathscr{N},\varphi)
is still the same. Finally, (
13.12
) implies

|\mathscr{X}|\leq\frac{|\mathscr{N}|-2}{g-1}
, meaning that again we reach a contradiction
to the choice of
(\mathscr{N},\varphi)
in
(0 )
.
∎

After these preparations we can quickly establish the main result of this subsection.

Proof of Theorem
13.12
.

Let
\Phi
be any linear Ramsey construction and let
\Xi
be a partite
lemma applicable to
k
-partite
k
-uniform hypergraphs
F
with
\mathrm{girth}(F)>n

that delivers linear systems of hypergraphs
(H,\mathscr{H})

satisfying
\mathrm{Girth}(H,\mathscr{H}^{+})>n
. We recall that the existence of such a partite
lemma is an immediate consequence of Theorem
10.19
.

Let us attempt to perform the partite construction

\mathrm{PC}(\Phi,\Xi)_{r}(F)=(H,\mathscr{H})
. By Lemma
13.14
picture zero is

(g,n)
-certified and an iterative application of Lemma
13.15

discloses that all further pictures are well-defined and, likewise,

(g,n)
-certified. In particular, the final picture is
well-defined and the fact that it is
(g,n)
-certified implies that
it has the desired property.
∎

Finally, we deduce the last statement announced in the introduction.

Proof of Theorem
1.6
.

Given a linear
k
-uniform hypergraph
F
and
r,n\in{\mathds{N}}
we apply
Theorem
1.7
with
n^{\prime}=\binom{n}{k}
instead of
n
, thus obtaining
some linear system
(H,\mathscr{H})
. Without loss of generality we can assume
that
E(H)=E(\mathscr{H})
, for deleting
edges from
H
that belong to none of the copies in
\mathscr{H}
cannot influence
whether the system
(H,\mathscr{H})
satisfies the conclusion of Theorem
1.7
.

In order to show that
H
has the desired property we consider any set

X\subseteq E(H)
whose size it at most
n
. For every edge
e
of
H

contained in
X
we fix some copy
F_{e}\in\mathscr{H}
such that
e\in E(F_{e})
.
Since there are at most
\binom{|X|}{k}
such edges, the set

\mathscr{N}^{-}=\bigl\{F_{e}\in\mathscr{H}\colon e\in E(H)\text{ and }e\subseteq X\bigr\}

has at most the size
n^{\prime}
. In the special case that
|\mathscr{N}^{-}|\leq 1

we can set
\mathscr{N}=\mathscr{N}^{-}
and are done. Otherwise the conclusion of Theorem
1.7

yields a set
\mathscr{X}\subseteq\mathscr{H}
such that
\mathscr{N}=\mathscr{N}^{-}\cup\mathscr{X}
is a forest
of copies with the desired property.
∎
